KIN 482E Final Project¶

Jiho Song (50317825)

Link to the Dataset¶

  • https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/stefanoleone992/fifa-22-complete-player-dataset?select=players_22.csv

Background Information¶

International Federation of Association Football (FIFA) is the international governing body of football (soccer), beach football, and futsal. Annually, FIFA collaborates with EA Sports to create a football game series named FIFA. Every active professional player has a card that lists their overall rating and 6 general statistics within the game. The overall rating is found at the top left corner of the card, while the 6 general statistics are listed underneath.

Specifically, the 6 general statistics for outfield players (non-goalkeepers) include: Shooting, Passing, Pace, Physical, Dribbling, and Defending.
Meanwhile, for goalkeepers, the categories are: Diving, Handling, Kicking, Positioning, Reflexes, and Speed.

The images below are an example of what a typical FIFA Card that is revealed to the public looks like.

Statistics and Its Concerns¶

The statistics are updated annually with the release of a new game series each year. The current dataset is from FIFA 22, reflecting player performances and characteristics from the 2021-22 soccer season. However, each time player ratings are published, they spark debates among fans and players.

Many question the criteria behind the overall ratings and other statistics, as the scores often seem unintuitive. Common questions include, “How does this player have a higher overall rating than another?” or “Where did this shooting rating come from?” Therefore, this project seeks to address these concerns by conducting a detailed analysis of the statistics and exploring the factors that might influence player ratings.

Purpose of the Project¶

Through this project, four general analyses will be accomplished:

  1. Conducting a more detailed analysis of the 6 general statistics.
  2. Understanding how the general statistics differ from the detailed statistics.
  3. Understanding the relationship between rating and value of players.
  4. Understanding the relationship between wage and position of players.

Detailed steps of the analysis are written within their sections.

Filtering the Data¶

Before we begin, it is important to remove any unnecessary columns and look at the data set. Then, we will further organize the data by relisting the rows from highest to lowest overall rating. We will call this data frame df.

Filtering Continued¶

Note that the dataset includes nearly 20,000 player records. However, since most interest centers around players in the most popular leagues, let's filter out those outside Europe's top five leagues. These five leagues include: English Premier League, Spanish La Liga, German Bundesliga, Italian Serie A, and French Ligue 1. Also, we will remove players whose position is substitution (SUB) or reserve (RES), as they do not play full-time for their clubs. We will name this filtered data frame df_filt.

Next, since these players are listed from highest to lowest overall rating, let’s add a column named "Rank" that assigns each player a rank from 1 to the end of the dataset. We will then set this new column as the index.

In [2]:
# Name the top 5 leagues
top_5_leagues = ['French Ligue 1', 'German 1. Bundesliga', 'English Premier League', 'Spain Primera Division', 'Italian Serie A']

# Filter players who are not in the top 5 leagues and those who are substitutions or reserves.
df_filt = df[df['league_name'].isin(top_5_leagues)]
df_filt = df_filt[~df_filt['club_position'].isin(['RES', 'SUB'])]

# Create a column named "Rank" and set it as index.
df_filt['Rank'] = range(1, len(df_filt) + 1)
df_filt = df_filt.set_index('Rank')
df_filt

Club Rankings¶

We’ll retrieve the club rankings for the five European leagues from the 2021-22 season, as this season represents the year on which FIFA 22 based its updates. Then, we will create a column named club_ranks, where each player’s club ranking is listed according to the team they play for. Most leagues consist of 20 teams, aside from the German league, which consists of 18 teams.

Analysis 1: Detailed Understanding of the General Statistics¶

We will first take a closer look at the 6 general statistics previously described. This will be accomplished by:

  1. Visualize the top 10 players in each of the 6 general statistics.
  2. Analyze which positions are dominant in each statistic.
  3. Analyze how the values of detailed statistics compare to the general statistics. (Here, detailed statistics refer to player statistics that are not visible on the player cards but are found in this data frame)

Firstly, let's visualize the top 10 players in each general statistic category and view their general descriptions.

What Can We Learn From This?¶

We see that for some general statistics, certain positions may be more dominant than others. However, because it is difficult to visualize the trend, let's plot the distribution. Firstly, because soccer has so many position names, we will simplify the categorization into Attackers, Midfielders, and Defenders. Then, to better understand the distribution, we will sample the top 100 players in each general statistic and determine the proportion of each position in the sample.

In [5]:
# Categorize the positions. 
Attack = ['CF','ST','RS','LS','RF','LF']
Mid = ['RM','LM','LCM','RCM','LW','RW','CDM','CAM','CM','LDM','RDM','LAM','RAM']
Defend = ['LCB','RCB','LB','RB','LWB','RWB','CB']

# Proportion of each position for shooting. 
shooting100 = df_filt[df_filt['club_position']!='GK'].sort_values('shooting', ascending=False).head(100)
shoot_attack = round(shooting100['club_position'].isin(Attack).sum() / 
               shooting100['club_position'].count() * 100, 0)
shoot_mid = round(shooting100['club_position'].isin(Mid).sum()/ 
               shooting100['club_position'].count()*100,0) 
shoot_defend = round(shooting100['club_position'].isin(Defend).sum()/ 
               shooting100['club_position'].count()*100,0) 

# Proportion of each position for passing. 
passing100 = df_filt[df_filt['club_position']!='GK'].sort_values('passing', ascending=False).head(100)
pass_attack = round(passing100['club_position'].isin(Attack).sum() / 
              passing100['club_position'].count() * 100, 0)
pass_mid = round(passing100['club_position'].isin(Mid).sum()/ 
              passing100['club_position'].count()*100,0)
pass_defend = round(passing100['club_position'].isin(Defend).sum()/ 
              passing100['club_position'].count()*100,0)

# Proportion of each position for dribbling. 
dribbling100 = df_filt[df_filt['club_position']!='GK'].sort_values('dribbling', ascending=False).head(100)
dribble_attack = round(dribbling100['club_position'].isin(Attack).sum() / 
                 dribbling100['club_position'].count() * 100, 0)
dribble_mid = round(dribbling100['club_position'].isin(Mid).sum()/ 
                 dribbling100['club_position'].count()*100,0)
dribble_defend = round(dribbling100['club_position'].isin(Defend).sum()/ 
                 dribbling100['club_position'].count()*100,0)

# Proportion of each position for pace. 
pace100 = df_filt[df_filt['club_position']!='GK'].sort_values('pace', ascending=False).head(100)
pace_attack = round(pace100['club_position'].isin(Attack).sum() / 
              pace100['club_position'].count() * 100, 0)
pace_mid = round(pace100['club_position'].isin(Mid).sum()/ 
              pace100['club_position'].count()*100,0)
pace_defend = round(pace100['club_position'].isin(Defend).sum()/ 
              pace100['club_position'].count()*100,0)

# Proportion of each position for physic. 
physical100 = df_filt[df_filt['club_position']!='GK'].sort_values('physic', ascending=False).head(100)
physic_attack = round(physical100['club_position'].isin(Attack).sum() / 
                physical100['club_position'].count() * 100, 0)
physic_mid = round(physical100['club_position'].isin(Mid).sum()/ 
                physical100['club_position'].count()*100,0)
physic_defend = round(physical100['club_position'].isin(Defend).sum()/ 
                physical100['club_position'].count()*100,0)

# Proportion of each position for defending. 
defending100 = df_filt[df_filt['club_position']!='GK'].sort_values('defending', ascending=False).head(100)
defend_attack = round(defending100['club_position'].isin(Attack).sum() / 
                defending100['club_position'].count() * 100, 0)
defend_mid = round(defending100['club_position'].isin(Mid).sum()/ 
                defending100['club_position'].count()*100,0)
defend_defend = round(defending100['club_position'].isin(Defend).sum()/ 
                defending100['club_position'].count()*100,0)
In [6]:
# Define our data. 
positions = ['Strikers', 'Midfielders', 'Defenders']
percentages_shoot = [shoot_attack, shoot_mid, shoot_defend]
percentages_pass = [pass_attack, pass_mid, pass_defend]
percentages_dribble = [dribble_attack, dribble_mid, dribble_defend]
percentages_pace = [pace_attack, pace_mid, pace_defend]
percentages_physic = [physic_attack, physic_mid, physic_defend]
percentages_defend = [defend_attack, defend_mid, defend_defend]

# Plot the distribution of positions for Shooting.
fig, axs = plt.subplots(3,2, figsize=[8,7])
axs[0,0].bar(positions, percentages_shoot)
for i, value in enumerate(percentages_shoot):
    axs[0, 0].text(i, value + 2, f"{value}%", ha='center', va='bottom')
axs[0,0].set(xlabel='Positions of Players', ylabel='Percentage of Positions')
axs[0,0].set_title('% of Player Positions in Top100 Shooting Stat', fontweight='bold', pad=20, fontsize=10)
axs[0,0].spines['top'].set_visible(False)
axs[0,0].spines['right'].set_visible(False)

for i, value in enumerate(percentages_pace):

axs[1,1].set(xlabel='Positions of Players', ylabel='Percentage of Positions')
axs[1,1].set_title('% of Player Positions in Top100 Pace Stat', fontweight='bold', pad=20, fontsize=10)
axs[1,1].spines['top'].set_visible(False)
axs[1,1].spines['right'].set_visible(False)

# Plot the distribution of positions for Physic.
axs[2,0].bar(positions, percentages_physic)
for i, value in enumerate(percentages_physic):
    axs[2, 0].text(i, value + 2, f"{value}%", ha='center', va='bottom')
axs[2,0].set(xlabel='Positions of Players', ylabel='Percentage of Positions')
axs[2,0].set_title('% of Player Positions in Top100 Physic Stat', fontweight='bold', pad=20, fontsize=10)
axs[2,0].spines['top'].set_visible(False)
axs[2,0].spines['right'].set_visible(False)

# Plot the distribution of positions for Defending.
axs[2,1].bar(positions, percentages_defend)
for i, value in enumerate(percentages_defend):
    axs[2, 1].text(i, value + 2, f"{value}%", ha='center', va='bottom')

Which Positions Are Dominant For Each Statistic?¶

In shooting and defending, we see that the greatest biases in player positions are present, as 0% of defenders are ranked in the top 100 for shooting, while 0% of strikers are ranked in the top 100 for defending. This makes sense because compared to other statistics, they can be considered the most "extreme" statistic due to their importance for specific positions. Meanwhile, midfielders dominate in other statistics, especially passing, dribbling, and pace, as they require the most running and utilization of those skills.

So, because midfielders dominate in most statistics, let's see if the same trend occurs for the top 100 players of the entire df_filt data frame.

In [7]:
# Retrieve top 100 players in the df_filt data frame. Then, calculate the proportions of each position.
top_100_general = df_filt.head(100)
general_attack = round(top_100_general['club_position'].isin(Attack).sum() / 
                 top_100_general['club_position'].count() * 100, 0)
general_mid = round(top_100_general['club_position'].isin(Mid).sum()/ 
                 top_100_general['club_position'].count()*100,0)
general_defend = round(top_100_general['club_position'].isin(Defend).sum()/ 
                 top_100_general['club_position'].count()*100,0)
general_percentages = [general_attack, general_mid, general_defend]

# Plot the distribution.
fig, axs = plt.subplots(figsize=[4,4])
axs.bar(positions, general_percentages)
for i, value in enumerate(general_percentages):
    axs.text(i, value + 1, f"{value}%", ha='center', va='bottom')
axs.set(xlabel='Positions of Players', ylabel='Percentage of Positions')
axs.set_title('% of Player Positions in Top100 Players', fontweight='bold', pad=20, fontsize=10)
axs.spines['top'].set_visible(False)
axs.spines['right'].set_visible(False)
plt.show()

As expected, we see that midfielders dominate among the top 100 players in the data frame.

Detailed Statistic vs General Statistic¶

As previously described, the df_filt data frame contains detailed statistics such as "attacking finishing" and "skill ball control" that are not visible on the FIFA cards. To address the frequent questions regarding how the statistics are calculated, we hypothesized that the average of detailed statistics would align with the values of general statistics.

To do this, we will retrieve the top 10 players of each general statistic and compare their values with the average of related detailed statistics. For instance, when analyzing the top 10 players in shooting, the average will be calculated using relevant detailed statistics such as "power_shot_power" and "attacking_finishing." Next, we will calculate the difference by subtracting the general statistic value from the average of the relevant detailed statistics and store the result in a new column named "Difference."

In [8]:
# Retrieve the top 10 players for shooting
shoot10 = df_filt[df_filt['player_positions']!='GK'].sort_values('shooting', ascending=False).head(10)

# Calculate the average detailed stat for shooting. 
shoot10['Average Shooting'] = shoot10[['attacking_finishing','attacking_volleys','power_shot_power', 
                                       'skill_fk_accuracy','power_long_shots']].mean(axis=1)

# Create the "Difference" column.
shoot10['Difference'] = shoot10['shooting'] - shoot10['Average Shooting']

# Display the data.
print('Comparing Shooting Stats')
display(shoot10[['short_name','shooting','Average Shooting', 'Difference']])

What Do We Observe?¶

The values show that pace, shooting, and physic have large mean differences between the general statistics and detailed statstics, while passing, dribbling, and defending are not as significant. To understand why this may be the case, we will focus on players whose differences exceed the average difference for each general statistic. By identifying those who deviate most from the typical trend, we hope to reveal interesting patterns or anomalies contributing to these larger differences.

It is important to mention that the general statistic column will be highlighted in orange, while the detailed statistic columns with values significantly different from the general statistic column will be highlighted in sky blue. We will define a large difference as a difference greater than 10.

In [15]:
# Retrieve players that have greater value in the Difference column that the mean for pace.

pace_difference_high = pace_difference_high[['short_name', 'movement_acceleration','movement_sprint_speed','movement_agility',
                      'movement_reactions','movement_balance', 'Average Pace', 'pace', 'Difference']]

# Define the highlighting function to highlight rows of interest
def highlight_columns(col):
    if col.name in ['movement_balance', 'movement_reactions', 'movement_agility']:
        color = 'skyblue'
    elif col.name in ['pace']: 
        color = 'orange'
    else:
        color = 'white'
    return ['background-color: {}'.format(color) for _ in col]

# Ensuring that all values are displayed cleanly
pace_difference_high['pace'] = pace_difference_high['pace'].astype(int)
pace_difference_high['Average Pace'] = pace_difference_high['Average Pace'].astype(int)
pace_difference_high['Difference'] = pace_difference_high['Difference'].astype(int)

# Apply styling to the DataFrame
styled_pace = pace_difference_high.style.apply(highlight_columns)

# Display the data
print('Detailed View of Pace')
styled_pace

Conclusion¶

As the coloured rows show, statistics with large differences, such as pace, shooting, and physic, tend to include at least one detailed statistic that deviates significantly from the others and its corresponding general statistic. In contrast, statistics with smaller differences, like passing, dribbling, and defending, are composed of detailed statistics that are relatively consistent.

This observation suggests that the general statistic is likely not calculated as a simple average of the detailed statistics, especially for categories with large differences. Instead, each detailed statistic is likely assigned a different weight or proportion in the calculation, reflecting its relative importance in contributing to the overall value.

Analysis 2: Relationship Between Overall Rating and 6 General Statistics¶

In addition to the general statistics, the overall rating is also a controversial metric whose origins many people question. To understand how the overall rating may be derived, we will follow these steps of analysis:

  1. Calculate the average of the 6 general statistics.
  2. Compare this value with the overall rating to determine if they match.
  3. If they do not match, analyze how the overall rating varies under different circumstances and identify a potential method for its calculation.

Calculating Average of 6 General Statistics¶

To accomplish this step, we will create a column named average_data in the df_filt data frame to store each player's calculated average general statistic. It is important to note that goalkeepers and non-goalkeepers have different statistical categories. Therefore, we need to calculate the averages using two distinct procedures to account for these differences.

In [21]:
# Create average_data for non-goalkeepers.
df_filt['average_data'] = round(
    df_filt.loc[df_filt['club_position'] != 'GK', ['pace', 'shooting', 'passing', 
                                                   'dribbling', 'defending', 'physic']].mean(axis=1), 0)

By checking for any missing value in the average_data column, we see that the columns with club position as GK have NaN. As previously described, this is because goalkeepers have separate general ratings.

Comparing Overall vs Average Data¶

To analyze how different the overall rating is from the averaged value, we will first see what proportions of average data are smaller, equal to, or larger than the overall rating.

In [25]:
print('The proportion that are equal is:', 
      round((df_filt['overall'] == df_filt['average_data']).sum()/(df_filt['average_data']).count() * 100,1))
print('The proportion that are greater is:', 
      round((df_filt['overall'] > df_filt['average_data']).sum()/(df_filt['average_data']).count() * 100,1))
print('The proportion that are less is:',
      round((df_filt['overall'] < df_filt['average_data']).sum()/(df_filt['average_data']).count() * 100,1))

The proportion that are equal is: 0.1
The proportion that are greater is: 99.7
The proportion that are less is: 0.2

Taking a Closer Look¶

Based on the calculations, 99.7% of players have an overall rating higher than the average of their six general statistics. Meanwhile, 0.1% have an overall rating equal to the average, and only 0.2% have an overall rating lower than the average.

So, let's examine the small proportion of players whose overall ratings are equal to or less than the average of their general statistics.

In [26]:
df_filt[df_filt['overall'] <= df_filt['average_data']][['short_name', 'overall','average_data', 'club_name', 
                                                        'league_name', 'club_position', 'club_rank']]

933 O. Etebo 72 73 Watford English Premier League CDM 19

We observe that players whose overall ratings are equal to or lower than their average data are part of teams that finished in the middle or near the bottom of the table (e.g., the club ranks 9/20, 19/20, and 17/20) during the 2021-22 season. Specifically, players with lower overall ratings than their average data belong to lower-ranked teams than the player with equal ratings.

To explore this further, let’s examine whether, in general, the difference between the average data and the overall rating is greater for players in the top 5 teams of the 5 European leagues compared to those in the bottom 5 teams. For this analysis, we will create two data frames named top_5_teams and bottom_5_teams, which include all teams that finished in the top 5 and the bottom 5 of their respective leagues.

In [27]:
# Define top 5 and bottom 5 teams in the leagues. (German league has 18 teams unlike others who have 20).
top_5_teams = df_filt[df_filt['club_rank']<=5]
bottom_5_teams = df_filt[
    ((df_filt['league_name'] == 'German 1. Bundesliga') & (df_filt['club_rank'] >= 14)) |
    ((df_filt['league_name'] != 'German 1. Bundesliga') & (df_filt['club_rank'] >= 16))]

Now that we have created the two data frames, we will calculate the difference between the overall rating and the average general statistics data for each player and store the results in a new column named difference. Then, we will groupby league name to compare the mean difference value between leagues.

print(top_result)

# Determine the difference between overall rating and average data for bottom 5 teams.
bottom_5_teams['difference'] = bottom_5_teams['overall'] - bottom_5_teams['average_data']

# Reorganize the index to match the order of the top_result data. 
bottom_result = bottom_5_teams.groupby('league_name')['difference'].mean().reindex(['English Premier League', 
                                                                                    'Spain Primera Division', 
                                                                                    'German 1. Bundesliga', 'Italian Serie A', 
                                                                                    'French Ligue 1'])
print(bottom_result)

What Can We Learn From This?¶

As expected from our previous analysis, both figures show that the overall rating is greater than the average of the general statistics. However, we observe that players from top-ranked teams exhibit a greater difference compared to low-ranked teams. Furthermore, while the differences among players from low-ranked teams are relatively consistent, the degree of difference for players on top teams is ordered the same as the league competitiveness: from most to least competitive—English, Spanish, German, Italian, and French leagues.

This trend may be observed because top teams in more competitive leagues typically generate higher revenue and are more sought after by world-class players. As a result, top teams in these leagues attract elite talent, significantly boosting their overall ratings. This is supported by the figure below, which demonstrates a moderate negative correlation of -0.59 between overall rating and club rank, indicating that as club rank increases (moving to lower-ranked teams), the overall rating of players tends to decrease. Furthermore, we could also infer that players who belong to higher-ranked teams may receive a "boost" in their overall rating because of the prestige and quality associated with their team.

Comparing Overall vs Average Detailed Statistics¶

Since our goal is to identify the best calculation method to determine how the overall rating is derived, let's explore whether we can reduce the difference by applying an alternative approach.

Below, we create a new column called average_detail_data by grouping players based on their positions: Attackers, Defenders, or Goalkeepers. Then, as we did before, we will retrieve detailed statistics not shown on the FIFA card and calculate averages for relevant statistics based on each position. Finally, we can compare these position-specific averages to each player's overall rating.

Continuing the Journey of Finding Where the Overall Data Comes From¶

As the overall rating continues to be larger, we attempted to reduce this gap by incorporating the potential boost observed in players from higher-ranked teams into the calculation. This was done by giving a 10-point bonus to the value of the average_detail_data for players belonging to the top 5 teams, an 8-point bonus for players of teams ranked between 6 to 10, and assigning 6 points for all other players. We then calculated the difference between the overall rating and this adjusted value, storing the result in a new column named new_difference.

In [38]:
# Assign team bonuses
df_filt['team_bonus'] = 0  
df_filt.loc[df_filt['club_rank'] <= 5, 'team_bonus'] = 10  
df_filt.loc[(df_filt['club_rank'] > 5) & (df_filt['club_rank'] <= 10), 'team_bonus'] = 8
df_filt.loc[df_filt['club_rank'] > 10, 'team_bonus'] = 6  

# Calculate new_difference with the team bonus as well as the mean and standard deviation of new_difference.
df_filt['new_difference'] = df_filt['overall'] - (df_filt['average_detail_data'] + df_filt['team_bonus'])
df_filt_result = np.abs(df_filt['new_difference'].mean())
df_filt_result2 = np.abs(df_filt['new_difference'].std())
print('The mean difference after calculation is:', round(df_filt_result, 1))
print('The standard deviation of the difference is:', round(df_filt_result2, 1))

The mean difference after calculation is: 0.1
The standard deviation of the difference is: 3.7

Conclusion¶

The calculations yielded a result with a mean difference of 0.1 from the actual overall rating, with a standard deviation of 3.7. This suggests that the approach provides a reasonable approximation of the method used to determine the overall rating.

Analysis 3: Relationship Between Rating and Value of Players¶

To understand the relationships that may be present between the ratings of the players and their value, we will analyze this through following steps:

  1. Plot and analyze the relationship between a player's overall rating and their value.
  2. If you rank players by value and overall rating, do they match?
  3. How does age influence the value of players?

Relationship Between Overall Rating and Value of Player¶

To understand this relationship, we will first plot the relationship between the overall rating and the value of each player. Next, we will extract the top 100 players based on their overall rating from the df_filt data frame, creating a new data frame called top_100. Finally, we will plot the same relationship using the top_100 data to identify any differences compared to the full dataset.

It is important to note that player values in the df_filt data vary significantly among players. Thus, we will apply a log10 transformation to the values for clearer analysis. However, due to this transformation, the y-axis does not represent the actual player values but rather the ratios between values.

In [39]:
# Log the value of players and store the result in log_value column.
df_filt['log_value'] = np.log10(df['value_eur'])

# Extract the top 100 players.
top_100 = df_filt.head(100)

# Plot the relationship for entire data.
fig, axs = plt.subplots(1,2, figsize=[10,4])
sns.regplot(data=df_filt, x='overall', y='log_value', scatter=False, color='red', line_kws={'linestyle': '--'}, ax=axs[0])
axs[0].set_xlabel('Overall Rating')
axs[0].set_ylabel('Value of Player in EUR (Log)')
axs[0].spines['top'].set_visible(False)
axs[0].spines['right'].set_visible(False)
axs[0].set_title('Overall rating vs. Value of Players (Entire Data)', fontweight='bold')

# Plot the relationship for top_100 data. Used log for easier comparison, although not needed for top_100 data.

axs[1].set_xlabel('Overall Rating')
axs[1].set_ylabel('Value of Player in EUR (Log)')
axs[1].spines['top'].set_visible(False)
axs[1].spines['right'].set_visible(False)
axs[1].set_title('Overall rating vs. Value of Players (Top 100)', fontweight='bold')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Notice how, when transitioning from the entire data frame to the top 100 data, the correlation coefficient decreases from a strong positive correlation of 0.8 to a moderate positive correlation of 0.6. Additionally, the top 100 data plot exhibits greater variance, indicating that the relationship between overall rating and player value becomes less consistent among the highest-rated players.

If you rank best players by value and overall rating, do they match?¶

To understand why the relationship between overall rating and player value becomes inconsistent among the highest-rated players, we will focus on the "best players" in the df_filt data frame. "Best players" are defined as players whose overall rating and value are considered upper-outliers according to Tukey's method. By analyzing this group, we can better understand the dynamics among elite players and how factors beyond ratings influence their value.

In [41]:
# Determining upper-outlier threshold for overall rating in df_filt.
q1 = df_filt['overall'].quantile(0.25)
q3 = df_filt['overall'].quantile(0.75)
iqr = q3 - q1

out_high = q3 + iqr*1.5
out_low = q1 - iqr*1.5

print(out_high)

89.0
In [42]:
# Determining upper-outlier threshold for value of player in df_filt.
q1 = df_filt['value_eur'].quantile(0.25)
q3 = df_filt['value_eur'].quantile(0.75)
iqr = q3 - q1

out_high = q3 + iqr*1.5
out_low = q1 - iqr*1.5

print(out_high)

52600000.0

We have identified that anything above an overall rating of 89 and a value of €52,600,000 are upper-outliers. Using these thresholds, we can define our best players as those who exceed these values, filtering the dataset accordingly.

df_filt[df_filt['outlier']==True][['overall','short_name','age','value_eur','nationality_name']]

Overall Rank vs Value Rank¶

We observe that the top 11 players in the data frame have been identified as outliers. Next, let's examine whether the overall rating ranking aligns with the ranking of these players' values. The overall rating and value are sorted in descending order, with the highest listed at the top. If the value rank and overall rank are the same, the line is coloured blue. If the value rank is higher than the overall rating rank, the line is coloured green; if the opposite is true, the line is coloured red.

In [44]:

y = x.reset_index()
y = y.set_index('overall').sort_index(ascending=False)
x['rank_value'] = range(1, len(x) + 1)  
y['rank_overall'] = range(1, len(y) + 1)
merged = pd.merge(x.reset_index(), y.reset_index(), on='short_name')
merged

From the figure above, we observe a general trend where most players are ranked higher in value compared to their overall rating, with only one player having the same ranking in both categories. This observation aligns with our earlier finding of an inconsistent relationship among top players. However, two players, L. Messi and R. Lewandowski, stand out by being ranked lower in value but higher in overall rating. Let’s take a closer look at these two players to explore this discrepancy further.

Conclusion¶

The general trend of an increase in overall rating leading to greater value is intuitive. However, discrepancies emerged when the best players were ranked by a value relative to their overall rating. This can be attributed to the influence of age, where some older players are assigned lower values despite their strong past and current performance, contributing to high overall ratings. In contrast, younger players in similar forms are valued more highly due to their potential for future growth and longevity in the sport.

Analysis 4: Relationship Between Wage and Position¶

Lastly, let's analyze the relationship between the wages of players and their position. We will do this by:

  1. Take a look at the distribution of wage in df_filt and use this information to either calculate mean or median wage for each position.
  2. Retrieve players with top 100 wages in the df_filt data and check which positions dominate within the top 100.
  3. Analyze which players are "overpaid" and "underpaid."

Density Distribution of Wage and Overall Rating¶

Observing the density distributions below shows that wages are positively skewed, while overall ratings are more normally distributed. To better represent the data, we will use the median for wages, as the median is less affected by outliers and skewed distributions. For overall ratings, which follow a more normal distribution, we will use the mean.

In [47]:

sns.kdeplot(data=df_filt, x='overall', color='blue', ax=axs[1])
axs[0].set_xlabel('Wage in EUR')
axs[0].set_title('Distribution of Wage in FIFA 22')
axs[1].set_xlabel('Overall Rating')
axs[1].set_title('Distribution of Overall Rating in FIFA 22')
plt.show()

Median Wage of Each Position¶

Now, let’s examine the median wage for each position. Again, for simplicity, we will categorize club positions into four broad groups: attackers, midfielders, defenders, and goalkeepers.

In [48]:
# Print the median wage for each position
print(f'The median wage of a attacker in is €{round(df_filt[df_filt["club_position"].str.contains("CF|ST|RS|LS|RF|LF", na=False)]["wage_eur"].median(), 1)}')
print(f'The median wage of a midfielder in EUR is €{round(df_filt[df_filt["club_position"].str.contains("RM|LM|LCM|RCM|LW|RW|CDM|CAM|CM|LDM|RDM", na=False)]["wage_eur"].median(),1)}')
print(f'The median wage of a defender in EUR is €{round(df_filt[df_filt["club_position"].str.contains("LCB|RCB|LB|RB|LWB|RWB|CB", na=False)]["wage_eur"].median(),1)}')
print(f'The median wage of a goalkeeper in EUR is €{round(df_filt[df_filt["club_position"].str.contains("GK", na=False)]["wage_eur"].median(),1)}')

The median wage of a attacker in is €37000.0
The median wage of a midfielder in EUR is €31000.0
The median wage of a defender in EUR is €27500.0
The median wage of a goalkeeper in EUR is €27000.0

Listing positions from highest to lowerst median wage: attacker -> midfielder -> defender -> goalkeeper

From this simple analysis, we can potentially assume that outfield positions (attack, mid, def) are favored over goalkeepers. However, to be sure, let's see if this sort of trend is observed among 100 players who earn the most wage.

Retrieving the Top 100 Wages¶

We will retrieve 100 players who earn the most in the data and name it rich_100.

In [49]:
# Top 100 wages. 
rich_100=df_filt.sort_values('wage_eur', ascending=False).head(100)

Position Distribution Within Top 100¶

Then, we can take a look at how the positions are distributed within the rich_100 data. We will generalize the categorization of positions into Attacker, Midfielders (Mid), Defenders (Def), and Goalkeeprs (GK). Then, we will plot the distribution.

In [50]:
# Categorize the positions.
Attack = round(rich_100['club_position'].str.contains('CF|ST|RS|LS|RF|LF', na=False).sum() / rich_100['club_position'].count() * 100,0)
Mid = round(rich_100['club_position'].str.contains('RM|LM|LCM|RCM|LW|RW|CDM|CAM|CM|LDM|RDM', na=False).sum() / rich_100['club_position'].count() * 100,0)
Def = round(rich_100['club_position'].str.contains('LCB|RCB|LB|RB|LWB|RWB|CB', na=False).sum() / rich_100['club_position'].count() * 100,0)
GK = round(rich_100['club_position'].str.contains('GK', na=False).sum() / rich_100['club_position'].count() * 100,0)
positions = ['Attack', 'Mid', 'Defense', 'GK']
data1 = [Attack,Mid,Def,GK]

# Plot the distribution. 
fig, axs = plt.subplots(figsize=[4,4])
axs.bar(positions, data1, color='skyblue')
for i, value in enumerate(data1):
    axs.text(i, value+0.5, f"{value}%", ha='center', va='bottom')
axs.set(xlabel='Positions of Players', ylabel='Percentage of Positions')
axs.set_title('% of Player Positions in Top 100 Wages', fontweight='bold', fontsize=10, pad = 20)
axs.spines['top'].set_visible(False)
axs.spines['right'].set_visible(False)
plt.show()

From the plot, we observe that midfielders dominate the rich_100 data, followed by defenders, attackers, and goalkeepers. This order does not align with the previous trend, which showed that the median wage decreases from attackers to midfielders, defenders, and goalkeepers. This suggests that while attackers generally earn the highest wages, the rich_100 data includes a larger number of midfielders and defenders, indicating that these positions may have a higher representation of moderately high earners.

Overpaid or Underpaid?¶

Now, let's see the distribution of underpaid and overpaid positions. We will define underpaid as those above the average overall rating within the rich_100 data but below the median wage. Meanwhile, those who are overpaid will be those below the average overall rating but above the median wage. Using this analysis, we can hopefully better understand the potential bias towards outfield players over goalkeepers.

In [51]:
# Calculating average overall rating and median wage. 
Average_overall = rich_100['overall'].mean()
Median_wage = rich_100['wage_eur'].median()
print(Average_overall)
print(Median_wage)

Wages and Distribution of Different Teams¶

Finally, let's see how the wage distribution changes among teams in different ranks. We will define top_teams as teams whose club ranks are less than or equal to 7, middle_teams as those ranked between 8 and 13, and bottom_teams as all other teams.

In [55]:
# Define the variables
top_5_teams = df_filt[df_filt['club_rank']<=7]
middle_teams = df_filt[(df_filt['club_rank']>7) & (df_filt['club_rank']<14)]
bottom_teams = df_filt[(df_filt['club_rank']>=14)]

# Plot the density distribution
fig, axs = plt.subplots(2,3, figsize=[12,6])
sns.boxplot(data=top_5_teams, x='wage_eur', color='red', ax=axs[0,0])
sns.boxplot(data=middle_teams, x='wage_eur', color='blue', ax=axs[0,1])
sns.boxplot(data=bottom_teams, x='wage_eur', color='green', ax=axs[0,2])
sns.kdeplot(data=top_5_teams, x='wage_eur', color='red', ax=axs[1,0])
sns.kdeplot(data=middle_teams, x='wage_eur', color='blue', ax=axs[1,1])
sns.kdeplot(data=bottom_teams, x='wage_eur', color='green', ax=axs[1,2])
axs[0,0].set_xlabel('Wage in EUR')
axs[0,0].set_title('Distribution of Wage in Top 5 Teams')
axs[0,1].set_xlabel('Wage in EUR')
axs[0,1].set_title('Distribution of Wage in Middle-Ranked Teams')
axs[0,1].tick_params(axis='x', rotation=90)
axs[0,2].set_xlabel('Wage in EUR')
axs[0,2].set_title('Distribution of Wage in Bottom-Ranked Teams')
axs[1,0].set_xlabel('Wage in EUR')
axs[1,1].set_xlabel('Wage in EUR')
axs[1,2].set_xlabel('Wage in EUR')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

As expected, higher-ranked teams earn greater wages, and we also observe a positively skewed distribution across all plots. This indicates that, in general, wages are unevenly distributed among all teams, with a much smaller number of players earning exceptionally high wages compared to the majority, who earn relatively similar wages.

There is an interesting trend where the number of outliers earning high wages increases as the team rank increases. This suggests that higher-ranked teams tend to have more evenly distributed player wages, while lower-ranked teams have multiple players earning significantly more than the upper quartile. This pattern aligns with lower-ranked teams' strategy, which may invest heavily in a few all-star players to enhance team quality. In contrast, higher-ranked teams typically consist of a larger roster of evenly compensated all-stars, contributing to their overall strength and balance.

Conclusion¶

From the comparison of wages and positions, we observe that outfield players are favoured over goalkeepers. Additionally, although higher-ranked teams contain more players who earn higher wages and have players with wages that are more evenly distributed, the positively-skewed distribution of wages among players is present in all groups.

Limitations¶

  • The ratings and statistics of players are likely influenced by their performance during the season. However, the current dataset lacks key performance metrics such as goals, assists, and match ratings, limiting the ability to analyze and hypothesize how overall ratings are calculated.
  • The value and ratings of players may also be influenced by the players' legacy. However, due to a lack of previous records of players, this also could not be accounted for.
  • Therefore, future research is recommended to include the player performance statistics and compare the current data set to previous data sets to grasp the full picture of the player and their statistics.
